text: This is the capstone for the whole course. Meridian Health Partners is a mid-size healthcare administration company, about two thousand employees, running claims processing, patient scheduling, and standard office IT. It's late in the year, and finance has just declared the annual change freeze. Here's what lands on IT's desk during an ordinary week in that stretch.

Three employees in one regional office can't reach the claims system — a VPN gateway is timing out, and this is the fourth time in two months. An employee requests a new laptop for a new hire starting Monday. A vendor security patch needs to go onto the patient-scheduling system, but it's December 18th, inside the freeze. A new technician keeps escalating simple password resets to second line. And once the freeze ends, the change manager notices VPN gateway failures account for a disproportionate share of all tickets in that period.

The gateway failure starts as an incident — restore access now — but the fourth repeat is also a problem-management flag, worth its own root-cause investigation. The laptop is a plain service request, fulfilled through the catalog, nothing broken. The security patch during a freeze is exactly what change enablement's emergency change path exists for — authorized even when a normal change would have to wait. The escalating technician points to a knowledge management and service desk gap, not a personal failing. And the post-freeze review is continual improvement: using data already being captured to plan a real fix.

Notice what was quietly present the whole time without its own situation: every one of these tickets runs against SLA timers, which is service level management, and that laptop is tracked from order to retirement by IT asset management. A real week doesn't hand you practices labeled one at a time — it hands you a pile of tickets, and recognizing which practice, often more than one, actually owns each one is the whole skill this course built toward.

That closes ITSM and ITIL 4 Foundations — the dimensions, the Service Value System, the value chain, and every core practice, now applied to one real organization. The next course in this path, ServiceNow Platform Fundamentals, is where you finally open the platform itself and put this vocabulary to work hands-on.
